author: augustine-of-hippo
fields.title: Confessions (For Teens)
fields.description: At sixteen, Augustine and his friends stole a tree's worth of pears they didn't even want and threw them to the pigs. Thirty years later, as a bishop, he wrote the whole story of his restless life as one long prayer to God: the lies, the ambition, the nine years in a strange religion, the woman he loved and sent away, the friend he lost, the mother who never stopped crying for him, and a child's voice in a garden in Milan. This teen edition retells the Confessions in plain English, quoting Augustine's own words throughout.
fields.hook: At sixteen he stole pears he didn’t even want. Thirty years later he told God the whole story.

qa.question: Who was Augustine?
qa.answer: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a North African, born in Thagaste in what is now Algeria. He was a brilliant teacher of public speaking who spent years chasing success, pleasure and answers. He became a Christian in Milan in 386, was baptised the next year, and later served for more than thirty years as bishop of Hippo, writing books that shaped Christian thinking for centuries.

qa.question: Is this book honest about the hard parts?
qa.answer: Yes. It keeps the stolen pears, the lies, the years in a religious movement he later rejected, and his sexual history: he lived for about fifteen years with a woman he never married, had a son with her, sent her away to make a better marriage, and took someone else. It names that plainly, and says plainly that sending her away was a wrong done to her.

qa.question: What does “our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee” mean?
qa.answer: It is from the first page of the Confessions. Augustine means that God made people for himself, so nothing smaller than God can satisfy them. Every chase in the book, after praise, pleasure, cleverness and love, is that restlessness at work until it finds rest in God.

qa.question: Did Augustine really pray “Give me chastity and continency, only not yet”?
qa.answer: Yes, by his own account, as a teenager. He tells it in Book VIII against himself: he was afraid God would answer quickly and take away desires he still wanted to satisfy. It has become the classic picture of putting off doing what you know is right.

qa.question: What happened in the garden in Milan?
qa.answer: In 386, torn between his old habits and God, Augustine wept under a fig tree and heard a child's voice chanting “Take up and read.” He opened Paul's letters at Romans 13:13–14, and his doubt vanished. His friend Alypius read the next verse and joined him.

qa.question: How did Augustine treat the people closest to him?
qa.answer: Both well and badly, and he says so. He was a loyal, warm friend, and he grieved deeply. But he lied to his mother to escape her at a harbour, and he sent away the faithful mother of his son. He confesses all of it without excuses and gives God the credit for whatever good there was.

qa.question: What is the Confessions, and why did Augustine write it?
qa.answer: A long prayer to God telling his life story, written around 397 to 400, when he was a bishop in his mid-forties. He wrote it to praise God's mercy, to tell honestly what he had been and what he still was, and to stir up his readers to turn to God. The quotations here are from E. B. Pusey's 1838 translation.

qa.question: What can a teenager take from it?
qa.answer: That restlessness is a signal, not a flaw; that crowds and habits can pull you further than you mean to go; that “not yet” has no end date; that people praying for you are not wasting their time; and that God is closer than you think: “Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.”

fields.title: Restless
fields.body_html:
“As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.” — Psalm 42:1 (KJV)

Most life stories begin with “I was born.” This one begins with a prayer. Augustine wrote the Confessions in his mid-forties, around the year 400, when he was already a bishop in North Africa. He did not write it to you. He wrote it to God, addressing him as “Thou” on almost every page, and you get to listen in. On the very first page he puts down the sentence the whole book hangs from:

“Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.”

Hold on to that line. Everything that follows is that sentence acted out by a gifted, funny, ambitious and deeply restless young man.

He was born in 354 in Thagaste, a small town in Roman North Africa (today Souk Ahras in Algeria). His mother, Monica, was a Christian. His father, Patricius, was not. Augustine doesn't remember being a baby, but he has watched babies, and he refuses to get sentimental about them: “Myself have seen and known even a baby envious; it could not speak, yet it turned pale and looked bitterly on its foster-brother.” His verdict: “The weakness then of infant limbs, not its will, is its innocence.” Babies are harmless because they are small, not because they are good.

Then came school, and school meant beatings. Little Augustine heard adults talk about a great God who could hear and help, so he prayed, “though small, yet with no small earnestness, that I might not be beaten at school.” He got beaten anyway, and his parents laughed about it. He is fair to both sides. He really was lazy, because he loved games more than lessons. But he noticed the hypocrisy too: “elder folks' idleness is called 'business'; that of boys, being really the same, is punished by those elders.”

He loved stories. He cried over Dido, the queen in Virgil's poem who killed herself when her lover sailed away, and looking back he finds that the saddest thing about the boy he was: he was “weeping the death of Dido for love to Aeneas, but weeping not his own death for want of love to Thee, O God.” Meanwhile he was lying to his tutors and parents, stealing food from the family table to buy his way into other boys' games, and cheating to win. “And is this the innocence of boyhood?” he asks. “Not so, Lord, not so.” The same sins, he says, just move up a size: from nuts, balls and pet sparrows to gold, land and power.

Yet he ends his childhood chapter by thanking God for the boy. That child loved truth, “hated to be deceived, had a vigorous memory, was gifted with speech, was soothed by friendship.” All of that was good. The problem was where he went looking: “For it was my sin, that not in Him, but in His creatures—myself and others—I sought for pleasures, sublimities, truths, and so fell headlong into sorrows, confusions, errors.”

You probably know the restless feeling. It's the reason you open an app, close it, and open it again. Augustine's claim is that the restlessness is not a fault in you to be fixed with more stuff. It is a homing signal. You were made for God, and nothing smaller will hold your weight.

One thing to do this week: one evening, notice the moment you reach for something to fill a quiet minute. Stop and ask yourself honestly: what am I actually hungry for right now? Then pray Augustine's first line in your own words: “You made me for yourself, and I'm restless until I rest in you.”

study_questions.question: What is the famous sentence on the first page of the Confessions?
study_questions.answer: “Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.” God made us for himself, and we stay restless until we rest in him.

study_questions.question: Why does Augustine say babies are not truly innocent?
study_questions.answer: Because he has watched a baby turn pale with envy at another child feeding. Their innocence, he says, is the weakness of their limbs, not the goodness of their will.

study_questions.question: What does he thank God for about his boyhood, and what does he call his sin?
study_questions.answer: He thanks God for the boy's love of truth, good memory, gift of speech and friendships. His sin was looking for pleasure and truth in created things instead of in God.

fields.title: Pears for the Pigs
fields.body_html:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9 (KJV)

When Augustine was sixteen, his schooling stopped for a year. His father, “but a poor freeman of Thagaste,” was scraping money together to send him to university in Carthage, and the town admired him for it. But Augustine notes that the same father “had no concern how I grew towards Thee, or how chaste I were,” as long as his son became a brilliant speaker. So Augustine had a year with no school, no structure and plenty of friends.

He is honest about what happened next. That year, sexual desire “took the rule over me, and I resigned myself wholly to it.” His mother took him aside and warned him privately “not to commit fornication; but especially never to defile another man's wife.” He thought these were “womanish advices, which I should blush to obey.”

Then he admits something that is almost painfully familiar. His friends bragged about what they had done, and he was embarrassed to be less bad than they were. So he made things up: “I would say that I had done what I had not done, that I might not seem contemptible in proportion as I was innocent; or of less account, the more chaste.” He lied to look worse than he was.

And then he tells the story everyone remembers:

“A pear tree there was near our vineyard, laden with fruit, tempting neither for colour nor taste. To shake and rob this, some lewd young fellows of us went, late one night (having according to our pestilent custom prolonged our sports in the streets till then), and took huge loads, not for our eating, but to fling to the very hogs, having only tasted them.”

That's it: some teenagers stole pears and threw them to the pigs. Why does a great thinker spend a whole section of his life story on it? Because he can't explain it. He wasn't hungry. He had better pears at home. He didn't even like these ones. “It was foul, and I loved it; I loved to perish, I loved mine own fault, not that for which I was faulty, but my fault itself.” He did it because it was forbidden. That is what frightens him.

He keeps digging, and he finds one more thing: he would never have done it alone. In his own words, “alone I had never done it.” The fun was in the group, in getting away with it together. “O friendship too unfriendly!” he writes, for “when it is said, 'Let's go, let's do it,' we are ashamed not to be shameless.”

But he doesn't leave it there. Looking back, he gives thanks “that Thou hast melted away my sins as it were ice.” And he tells readers who never did anything like this not to look down on him. If they were kept from it, that was God's mercy too.

You have probably done something in a group that you would never have done on your own: a joke that went too far, a message you forwarded, a dare. Augustine isn't saying your friends are bad. He's saying that sin loves an audience, and that the human heart can want wrong things simply because they are wrong. That's not a reason to despair. It's a reason to stop trusting the crowd's “Let's go” and to bring your heart to the one who can melt it.

One thing to do this week: the next time a group says “Let's go, let's do it,” pause long enough to ask: would I do this if I were alone? If the answer is no, be the one who says, “I'm out.”

study_questions.question: Why did Augustine and his friends steal the pears?
study_questions.answer: Not because they were hungry or wanted the pears. They threw most of them to the pigs. They did it because it was forbidden and because they enjoyed doing wrong together.

study_questions.question: What lie did Augustine tell his friends at sixteen?
study_questions.answer: He boasted about sins he had not actually committed, because he was ashamed to seem more innocent than they were.

study_questions.question: What does Augustine mean by “friendship too unfriendly”?
study_questions.answer: A friendship that pulls you into doing harm. He says he would never have stolen the pears alone; the group made him “ashamed not to be shameless.”

fields.title: A Cauldron of Unholy Loves
fields.body_html:
“Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 18:3 (KJV)

At seventeen Augustine arrived in Carthage, the biggest city in Roman Africa. He describes it in one of his most famous lines: “To Carthage I came, where there sang all around me in my ears a cauldron of unholy loves.” He wasn't in love with anyone yet. He was in love with the idea of being in love: “I loved not yet, yet I loved to love.” When he did get what he wanted, it came with “jealousy, and suspicions, and fears, and angers, and quarrels.”

He also loved the theatre, especially tragedies. He noticed something odd about himself: he paid money to feel sad. Of the theatre-goer he writes, “this very sorrow is his pleasure.” He wept for characters who weren't real, while doing nothing for people who were. If you have ever binged a show that left you emotionally wrecked and wanting more, you know what he means.

At school he was a star, top of the rhetoric class, and proud of it. Carthage had a student gang who called themselves the Subverters, whose idea of fun was mocking and harassing newcomers. Augustine didn't join in, and he hated what they did. But he hung around with them anyway, “with a shameless shame that I was not even as they.”

Then, at eighteen, something real happened. His father had died two years before, and in a set reading for class he came across a book by the Roman writer Cicero called Hortensius, which urged people to love wisdom above everything. It changed him. “But this book altered my affections, and turned my prayers to Thyself O Lord.” He says, “How did I burn then, my God, how did I burn to re-mount from earthly things to Thee.” Only one thing held him back: “the name of Christ was not in it.” He had taken in that name “with my mother's milk,” and anything without it couldn't fully hold him.

So he opened the Bible. And he was disappointed. Compared with Cicero's polished Latin, the Scriptures looked plain and simple, and “my swelling pride shrunk from their lowliness.” The Bible, he later realised, is the kind of book that grows up with a person who is willing to be little. “But I disdained to be a little one; and, swollen with pride, took myself to be a great one.”

Instead he joined the Manichees, a religious movement founded in Persia about a century before. They promised clever answers for everything: the world was a battlefield between two powers, Light and Darkness, and when you sinned it wasn't really you, but the dark part mixed into you. They talked about truth constantly. “Yet they cried out 'Truth, Truth,' and spake much thereof to me, yet it was not in them.” Augustine, the brilliant student, ended up believing things like that “a fig-tree wept when it was plucked.” He stayed with them for nine years.

Even then, he says, God was closer than he knew: “But Thou wert more inward to me than my most inward part; and higher than my highest.”

Being clever is not the problem. Augustine was one of the sharpest minds of his age. The problem was pride: he wanted a truth that matched his own sophistication, and he skipped over the one that asked him to bow. Jesus said the kingdom belongs to those who become like little children. That isn't a call to stop thinking. It's a call to stop thinking you are too big to be taught.

One thing to do this week: read one short chapter of a Gospel, such as Mark 1, slowly. Write down one thing you understand and one thing you don't. Read it as someone willing to be “a little one,” not as a critic.

study_questions.question: What book first turned Augustine toward God, and what was missing from it?
study_questions.answer: Cicero's Hortensius, which made him burn with love for wisdom. What was missing was the name of Christ.

study_questions.question: Why was Augustine disappointed when he first read the Bible?
study_questions.answer: It seemed plain next to Cicero's style, and his pride “shrunk from their lowliness.” He refused to become a “little one” who could grow into it.

study_questions.question: What did the Manichees teach about sin, and why might that be attractive?
study_questions.answer: That sin was done by a dark nature mixed into a person, not really by the person. It let Augustine feel free from blame.

fields.title: The Son of These Tears
fields.body_html:
“They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.” — Psalm 126:5 (KJV)

Monica took her son's new religion very hard. For a while she would not even let him eat at her table. Augustine says she wept for him “more than mothers weep the bodily deaths of their children,” because she believed he was dying in a deeper way.

Then she had a dream. She was standing on a wooden ruler, crying, when a bright young man came up smiling and asked why she was so sad. She told him she was grieving for her son. He told her to look, and see “That where she was, there was I also.” She looked, and there was Augustine, standing on the ruler beside her.

When she told him, Augustine had a clever answer ready: the dream obviously meant that she would one day come round to his view. She answered at once: “No; for it was not told me that, 'where he, there thou also'; but 'where thou, there he also'.” Years later he admits that her quick reply shook him more than the dream did.

But nothing changed quickly. Nine more years went by. Monica asked a bishop who had once been a Manichee himself to talk her son out of it. The bishop refused. Augustine was too proud and too pleased with his arguments to be argued with, he said: “let him alone a while ... only pray God for him, he will of himself by reading find what that error is.” Monica would not stop begging, and she cried. At last the bishop, a little annoyed, sent her away with a sentence she treasured for the rest of her life: “Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.”

Meanwhile Augustine's life went on. He became a teacher of rhetoric, which he describes bluntly: he “made sale of a loquacity to overcome by.” He sold students the skill of winning arguments. And he was living with a woman he had not married. He names this plainly:

“In those years I had one,—not in that which is called lawful marriage, but whom I had found out in a wayward passion, void of understanding; yet but one, remaining faithful even to her.”

They were together for about fifteen years. Arrangements like this were common and accepted in the Roman world, but Augustine does not pretend it was what God intended. They had a son, Adeodatus, whose name in Latin means given by God. Augustine never tells us her name. He does say something honest about the child, that in such a relationship “children are born against their parents' will, although, once born, they constrain love.” Adeodatus wasn't planned. He was loved anyway.

So here is the picture in his early twenties: a brilliant young teacher, a partner and a little boy, a religion that flattered his mind, and a mother crying in church every morning and evening, year after year.

Maybe someone is praying for you like that right now: a parent, a grandparent, someone at church. Maybe it annoys you. Or maybe you are the one praying, for a friend or a brother or a parent, and nothing seems to be happening. Monica's story says two things. First, prayers can take years, and that does not mean they are lost. Second, sometimes the wisest thing is not another argument. The bishop's advice was simple: let him read, and pray.

One thing to do this week: write down the name of one person you have quietly given up on. Pray for them by name every day this week, without lecturing them. Or, if someone has been praying for you, thank them.

study_questions.question: What did Monica see in her dream, and how did she answer Augustine's reading of it?
study_questions.answer: She saw him standing beside her on a wooden ruler. When he said it meant she would come round to his view, she answered that it said “where thou, there he also,” not the other way round.

study_questions.question: What did the bishop say to Monica when she would not stop begging?
study_questions.answer: “Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.”

study_questions.question: How does Augustine describe the woman he lived with?
study_questions.answer: As a partner he had not married, found “in a wayward passion,” but only one, and he was faithful to her. They had a son, Adeodatus. He never gives her name.

Augustine was too proud and too pleased with his arguments to be argued with, he said: “let him alone a while ... only pray God for him, he will of himself by reading find what that error is.” Monica would not stop begging, and she cried. At last the bishop, a little annoyed, sent her away with a sentence she treasured for the rest of her life: “Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.” Meanwhile Augustine's life went on. He became a teacher of rhetoric, which he describes bluntly: he “made sale of a loquacity to overcome by.” He sold students the skill of winning arguments. And he was living with a woman he had not married. He names this plainly: “In those years I had one,—not in that which is called lawful marriage, but whom I had found out in a wayward passion, void of understanding; yet but one, remaining faithful even to her.” They were together for about fifteen years. Arrangements like this were common and accepted in the Roman world, but Augustine does not pretend it was what God intended. They had a son, Adeodatus, whose name in Latin means given by God. Augustine never tells us her name. He does say something honest about the child, that in such a relationship “children are born against their parents' will, although, once born, they constrain love.” Adeodatus wasn't planned. He was loved anyway. So here is the picture in his early twenties: a brilliant young teacher, a partner and a little boy, a religion that flattered his mind, and a mother crying in church every morning and evening, year after year. fields.title: Half of My Soul
fields.body_html:
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.” — Psalm 42:5 (KJV)

Back home in Thagaste, teaching his first classes, Augustine became inseparable from a friend he had grown up with. They had been at school together and played together. Augustine had pulled him into the Manichees too. He calls this friendship “sweet to me above all sweetness of that my life.” It lasted barely a year.

The friend fell ill with a high fever and lay unconscious for a long time. Because no one expected him to live, he was baptised while he was out cold. Augustine didn't care; he assumed his friend would laugh at it later. Then the friend woke up and began to recover. Augustine made a joke about the baptism, expecting him to join in. Instead, his friend “so shrunk from me, as from an enemy” and told him that if he wanted to stay friends, he must never talk like that again. Augustine was stunned. He decided to wait until his friend was stronger and then argue him out of it. A few days later, while Augustine was away, the fever came back, and his friend died.

What follows is one of the most honest pictures of grief ever written. “At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death.” His home town became torture, because every place reminded him. “Mine eyes sought him every where, but he was not granted them.” He told his soul to trust in God, and his soul refused, because the God he believed in then was a fantasy, and his friend had been real. “I became a great riddle to myself.”

He borrows the words of an old writer who called his friend “Thou half of my soul,” and says that was how it felt: “therefore was my life a horror to me, because I would not live halved.” And he describes something that many grieving people know: “at once I loathed exceedingly to live and feared to die.”

If you have ever felt that, that you don't want to go on living after a loss, please don't carry it alone. Tell a safe person this week: a parent, a pastor, a teacher, a doctor, or a crisis line where you live. Augustine survived his darkest year, and he did it with other people around him.

He couldn't stay in Thagaste, so he went back to Carthage. Slowly, time and friends patched him up. He lists what he loved in them: “to talk and jest together, to do kind offices by turns; to read together honied books; to play the fool or be earnest together.” Friendship, for him, was one of life's great gifts.

But looking back, he understood why the loss had nearly destroyed him: “I had poured out my soul upon the dust, in loving one that must die, as if he would never die.” His answer is not to love people less. It is to love them in a way that is held by something that can't be lost: “Blessed whoso loveth Thee, and his friend in Thee, and his enemy for Thee. For he alone loses none dear to him, to whom all are dear in Him who cannot be lost.”

This doesn't mean Christians don't grieve. Later in this book you'll see Augustine weep for his mother. It means that if your friendships rest in God, death is not the end of them. Your friends are not meant to be your god. They're meant to be loved, and held, in God's hands.

One thing to do this week: if you are grieving someone, tell one person their name and one memory of them. If you aren't, think of a friend who has lost someone this year and send them a message that simply says you remember.

study_questions.answer: He drew back “as from an enemy” and told Augustine to stop if he wanted to stay his friend.

study_questions.question: Why did Augustine say his grief was so crushing?
study_questions.answer: Because he had “poured out my soul upon the dust,” loving a person who must die as if he would never die, with no hope beyond this life.

study_questions.question: What way of loving friends does Augustine recommend instead?
study_questions.answer: To love God, and your friend in God, and even your enemy for God's sake, because then you lose no one who is dear to you.

fields.title: A Lie at the Harbour
fields.body_html:
“A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.” — Proverbs 16:9 (KJV)

For nine years the Manichees had told Augustine to wait for Faustus. Whenever he asked a hard question, especially about the stars, which their books described in ways that didn't match the astronomers' calculations, they said, Faustus will explain everything. When Augustine was twenty-eight, Faustus finally came to Carthage.

He was charming and a beautiful speaker. But Augustine had learned something by then: a thing is not “true, because eloquent.” When he finally got Faustus alone with his questions, he found that the great man knew almost nothing about the subjects in question. What surprised him was how Faustus handled it. “For he knew that he knew not these things, and was not ashamed to confess it.” Augustine liked him more for it: “For fairer is the modesty of a candid mind, than the knowledge of those things which I desired.” But his trust in the Manichees was broken. Faustus, he says, “neither willing nor witting it,” had begun to set him free.

Then Augustine decided to move to Rome. Friends promised him more money and prestige, but his main reason was the students. In Carthage they would “burst in audaciously” on other teachers' classes and wreck them. In Rome, people said, students behaved.

Monica did not want him to go. She followed him down to the harbour, clinging to him, determined either to stop him or to come too. So he lied to her. He told her he had to stay with a friend until the friend's ship could sail. “And I lied to my mother, and such a mother, and escaped.” He persuaded her to spend the night at a chapel near the ship, built in memory of Cyprian, an earlier bishop of Carthage. She spent it in tears and prayer. In the night he sailed.

“The wind blew and swelled our sails, and withdrew the shore from our sight; and she on the morrow was there, frantic with sorrow, and with complaints and groans filled Thine ears, Who didst then disregard them.”

That night Monica asked God for one thing: don't let him sail. God said no. But Augustine sees what was going on: God “regardest not what she then asked, that Thou mightest make me what she ever asked.” She prayed for him to stay; what she had always prayed for was his soul, and the road to that answer went through Italy.

In Rome he almost died. A fever brought him close to death, and this time, unlike when he was a sick little boy, he didn't even want to be baptised. He recovered. He also admits the real reason the Manichees still appealed to him: “it delighted my pride, to be free from blame.” When he did wrong, he could say it was some other nature in him. “But in truth it was wholly I.”

Then a job came up: the city of Milan needed a public professor of rhetoric. Augustine applied, gave a trial speech, and got it.

Two things to take from this. First, God's “no” is not the same as God not caring. Monica's worst night was part of the answer to her lifelong prayer. Second, watch for the phrase “it wasn't really me.” Augustine had a whole religion built around that excuse, and he says it kept him sick. Owning what you did is where healing starts.

One thing to do this week: think of a time you said, even to yourself, “that wasn't really me.” Say instead, to God or to the person involved: “That was me, and I'm sorry.”

study_questions.answer: Faustus knew he didn't know the answers and wasn't ashamed to admit it. Augustine called that “the modesty of a candid mind.”

study_questions.question: How did Augustine get away from his mother at the harbour?
study_questions.answer: He lied, saying he had to stay with a friend until the friend sailed. While she prayed through the night at a chapel near the ship, he sailed for Rome.

study_questions.question: How does Augustine explain God refusing Monica's prayer that night?
study_questions.answer: God ignored what she asked in that moment in order to give her what she had always asked: her son's salvation.

fields.title: To Milan I Came
fields.body_html:
“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” — Romans 10:17 (KJV)

“To Milan I came, to Ambrose the Bishop, known to the whole world as among the best of men.” Augustine was about thirty. Ambrose was the most important church leader in northern Italy, and he welcomed this young African professor warmly. “That man of God received me as a father.” Augustine started to love him, but not because he believed what Ambrose taught. He loved him because Ambrose was kind to him.

So he went to hear Ambrose preach every Sunday, purely as a professional, to judge whether his speaking lived up to the hype. He cared about style, not content. But you can't take in a man's words and keep out his meaning. “And while I opened my heart to admit 'how eloquently he spake,' there also entered 'how truly he spake'; but this by degrees.”

Ambrose showed him that Old Testament stories which had seemed crude or absurd could be read more deeply. He often repeated Paul's words, “The letter killeth, but the Spirit giveth life.” Augustine discovered something else too: the Church did not teach that God has a human-shaped body, which the Manichees had always mocked it for. He writes that “with joy I blushed at having so many years barked not against the Catholic faith, but against the fictions of carnal imaginations.” He had spent a decade attacking a cartoon.

He longed to talk to Ambrose properly, but he never got the chance. Crowds of people with problems always surrounded the bishop. Any spare moments Ambrose spent reading, and Augustine noticed something that amazed him: Ambrose read silently. He watched how “his eye glided over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest.” Augustine and his friends would sit quietly watching him read, then leave without daring to interrupt.

Augustine left the Manichees, but he didn't become a Christian yet. He decided to stay a catechumen, someone learning the faith, “till something certain should dawn upon me.” He began to see how much he already took on trust: history, faraway cities, the word of friends and doctors, and even “of what parents I was born, which I could not know, had I not believed upon hearsay.” Believing was not the opposite of thinking. Everyone did it.

Then Monica arrived. She had crossed the sea after him, and when a storm frightened the sailors she comforted them, sure that God had promised her a safe arrival. When Augustine told her he was no longer a Manichee, she was calm. She told him “She believed in Christ, that before she departed this life, she should see me a Catholic believer.”

In Africa, Monica used to bring cakes, bread and wine to the shrines of the martyrs. Ambrose had banned the custom in Milan, partly because some people got drunk at it. When the doorkeeper told her, she gave it up at once, without arguing. Ambrose, for his part, kept praising her to Augustine and congratulating him on having such a mother, “not knowing what a son she had in me.”

Sometimes the person who moves you toward God doesn't win an argument. They are just kind to you, and you keep showing up. And sometimes what you're rejecting about Christianity isn't Christianity at all, but a cartoon of it you picked up somewhere.

One thing to do this week: pick one thing about Christianity you've always found hard to accept. Before you decide again, find out what the church actually teaches about it: ask a pastor, or read a careful explanation, not a mocking summary from someone who never read it.

study_questions.answer: To judge his speaking style as a professional. He wasn't interested in the content at first, but the truth came in along with the eloquence.

study_questions.question: What did Augustine discover he had been attacking for years?
study_questions.answer: A false picture of the faith. The Church didn't teach that God has a human-shaped body; he had “barked” against “the fictions of carnal imaginations.”

study_questions.question: How did Monica respond when Ambrose banned her custom of bringing food and wine to martyrs' shrines?
study_questions.answer: She gave it up immediately and willingly, without arguing, and gave to the poor instead.

fields.title: Absent While Present
fields.body_html:
“Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.” — 1 Corinthians 15:33 (KJV)

In Milan, Augustine's career was going well. One day he was preparing a speech in praise of the emperor, a speech “wherein I was to utter many a lie, and lying, was to be applauded by those who knew I lied.” On the way, he passed a beggar in the street who had clearly had a few drinks, laughing and joking, completely carefree.

It hit him hard. “And certainly he was joyous, I anxious; he void of care, I full of fears.” With a few coins the beggar had got a cheap version of the happiness Augustine was chasing through all his scheming and ambition. And the beggar would sleep off his drunkenness that night. Augustine would wake up with his ambition the next day, and the next.

His closest friend in Milan was Alypius, a younger man from his home town who had once been his student. In Carthage, Alypius had been obsessed with the chariot races. One day Augustine, teaching, made a sarcastic comparison to people addicted to the races, not even thinking of Alypius. Alypius took it personally, not as an insult but as a wake-up call, and quit going.

But later, studying law in Rome, Alypius ran into something worse. Some friends coming back from dinner grabbed him and dragged him, protesting, into the amphitheatre to watch the gladiators fight and die. He told them:

“Though you hale my body to that place, and there set me, can you force me also to turn my mind or my eyes to those shows? I shall then be absent while present, and so shall overcome both you and them.”

He sat down and shut his eyes. Then a man fell in the arena, the whole crowd roared, and curiosity got him. He opened his eyes. “For so soon as he saw that blood, he therewith drunk down savageness; nor turned away, but fixed his eye, drinking in frenzy, unawares, and was delighted with that guilty fight.” In one afternoon he changed: “Nor was he now the man he came, but one of the throng he came unto.” He went back again and again, and dragged others along. His soul was “bold rather than resolute,” Augustine says, and “the weaker, in that it had presumed on itself, which ought to have relied on Thee.”

God did free Alypius from it in the end. By the time he was in Milan he had become a man of unusual integrity. As a legal adviser he turned down a bribe from a powerful senator and ignored his threats. But Augustine wants you to see the arena scene clearly, because it's about more than Rome.

You don't have gladiators. You do have a phone that can show you anything: violence, cruelty, porn, people being humiliated for laughs. And you may have friends who say, “Just watch this.” Alypius thought he was strong enough to sit there and stay untouched. He wasn't. Nobody is. What you keep looking at, you start to become. The strength Augustine recommends isn't bragging that you can handle it. It's knowing you can't, and leaning on God instead.

One thing to do this week: name one thing you watch or scroll that leaves you feeling like “one of the throng.” Skip it completely this week. If friends push, say what Alypius should have said: “I'm not watching that.”

study_questions.question: What did the drunk beggar make Augustine realise?
study_questions.answer: That the beggar had a cheap, short-lived happiness while Augustine, chasing praise through lies and ambition, had none at all, and was full of anxiety.

study_questions.question: What did Alypius promise he would do in the amphitheatre, and what actually happened?
study_questions.answer: He said he would be “absent while present” by keeping his eyes shut. When the crowd roared he opened them, saw the blood, and was gripped by it.

study_questions.question: According to Augustine, why did Alypius fall?
study_questions.answer: Because he trusted in his own strength. His soul was “bold rather than resolute,” and relied on itself instead of on God.

fields.title: Torn and Bleeding
fields.body_html:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” — John 1:14 (KJV)

Augustine turned thirty “sticking in the same mire.” He had big plans: a government post, influential friends, and “a wife with some money.” His mother worked hard to arrange a marriage for him, hoping that once he was married he would be baptised. A girl was found and asked for in marriage. She was two years under the legal age for marriage, so the wedding had to wait. Then he tells us what happened to the woman he had lived with since he was a student:

“Meanwhile my sins were being multiplied, and my concubine being torn from my side as a hindrance to my marriage, my heart which clave unto her was torn and wounded and bleeding. And she returned to Afric, vowing unto Thee never to know any other man, leaving with me my son by her.”

Read that slowly. They had been together for about fifteen years. She had been faithful to him. She was the mother of his son. And she was sent away because she was in the way of a career marriage. She went back to Africa without her child. Augustine doesn't tell us why he didn't simply marry her, and we shouldn't invent a reason. But we can say plainly what he himself suggests: this was a wrong done to her. He grieved, but she paid the price.

Then he makes it worse. She made a vow to God and kept it. He couldn't even wait two years for his wedding. He “procured another, though no wife.” He admits he “could not imitate a very woman”: the woman he had sent away was more faithful than he was. And the wound didn't heal; it went numb. His pains, he says, “became less acute, but more desperate.”

At the same time his mind was finally clearing. His great question had always been “whence is evil?” If God is good and made everything, where does evil come from? Some books of the Platonist philosophers gave him a new way to look. He turned inward and glimpsed something he could only call “the Light Unchangeable,” above his mind, the source of all truth. And he worked out that evil is not a thing at all, not a dark substance as the Manichees taught: “whatsoever is, is good.” Evil is what happens when something good gets twisted. “I enquired what iniquity was, and found it to be no substance, but the perversion of the will, turned aside from Thee.”

But something was missing from those books. They spoke of God's Word, the light of all people. “But that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, I read not there.” They described the goal but not the road, and they had nothing about humility. Augustine could now talk about God like an expert, but he says, “I did not hold to my Lord Jesus Christ, I, humbled, to the Humble.” Knowing about God was not the same as coming to him.

Notice how the two halves of this chapter fit together. Augustine's head was getting closer to God at the very moment his life was hurting someone badly. Clever thoughts about God did not stop him treating a faithful woman as disposable. Only a God who came down, made flesh, humble enough to touch real lives, could reach that.

If you have treated someone as if they didn't matter, a friend you dropped for a better group, or someone you used, don't dress it up. Augustine didn't. He called it his sins being multiplied.

fields.title: Only Not Yet
fields.body_html:
“For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.” — Romans 7:19 (KJV)

By now Augustine's doubts were mostly gone. He says, “nor did I now desire to be more certain of Thee, but more steadfast in Thee.” His problem wasn't his head any more. It was his will. “But still I was enthralled with the love of woman.”

He went to see Simplicianus, an old priest who had been like a father to Ambrose. Simplicianus told him about Victorinus, a famous professor in Rome, so honoured that he had a statue in the Forum. Victorinus had secretly been studying the Bible and told Simplicianus, “Understand that I am already a Christian.” Simplicianus replied, “I will not believe it, nor will I rank you among Christians, unless I see you in the Church of Christ.” Victorinus joked, “Do walls then make Christians?” He was afraid of what his powerful pagan friends would say. But eventually he said, “Go we to the Church; I wish to be made a Christian.” When he stood up to declare his faith publicly, the congregation recognised him, and a murmur ran through the crowd: “Victorinus! Victorinus!”

Augustine was “on fire to imitate him.” But he couldn't. He explains exactly why, in a passage about habit that might be the most useful thing he ever wrote:

“My will the enemy held, and thence had made a chain for me, and bound me. For of a forward will, was a lust made; and a lust served, became custom; and custom not resisted, became necessity.”

A wrong want, given in to, becomes a habit. A habit, never fought, becomes something you feel you can't live without. He compares himself to someone lying in bed in the morning who knows he should get up but keeps sinking back into sleep. When God called him, he had only “those dull and drowsy words, 'Anon, anon,' 'presently,' 'leave me but a little.'” But “'presently, presently,' had no present, and my 'little while' went on for a long while.”

Then a visitor named Pontitianus, an African official at the emperor's court, noticed a copy of Paul's letters on Augustine's table and started talking about Antony, the Egyptian monk who had given away everything to follow Christ. He told how two of his colleagues had found a book about Antony's life in a cottage and read it, and one of them turned to the other and said, “But a friend of God, if I wish it, I become now at once.” Both gave up their careers on the spot.

As Pontitianus talked, Augustine felt God turning him around to face himself, “that I might see how foul I was.” He remembered a prayer he had prayed years before, at the very start of his youth, and it shamed him:

“Give me chastity and continency, only not yet.”

“For I feared lest Thou shouldest hear me soon,” he explains, “and soon cure me of the disease of concupiscence, which I wished to have satisfied, rather than extinguished.”

“Only not yet” might be the most honest prayer anyone has ever written down. Maybe it's yours. It could be about porn, vaping, gaming till 3 a.m., a relationship you know is wrong, or a lie you keep up. You know what's right. You even want to want it. Just not yet. Augustine's warning is that “not yet” has no end date. Habit doesn't wait for you to be ready. It just gets stronger.

One thing to do this week: name your own “not yet.” Take one concrete step against it today, not next week: delete the app, throw it out, end the conversation. Then tell one person you trust what you're doing.

study_questions.question: How does Augustine describe the way a habit becomes a chain?
study_questions.answer: A wrong will becomes a desire; a desire given in to becomes a habit; and a habit not resisted becomes something that feels like necessity.

study_questions.question: Why did the teenage Augustine pray “only not yet”?
study_questions.answer: Because he was afraid God would answer quickly and take away desires he still wanted to satisfy.

fields.title: Take Up and Read
fields.body_html:
“But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.” — Romans 13:14 (KJV)

When Pontitianus left, Augustine turned on Alypius, half shouting. “What ails us?” Ordinary people with no education were giving their lives to God, while the two of them, with all their learning, were still stuck. His face said more than his words. Then he rushed out into the small garden of the house where they were staying. Alypius followed and sat down quietly near him.

What happened in that garden is the centre of the whole book. Augustine was at war with himself. He found it strange: he could tell his hand to move and it moved at once, but he couldn't get his own will to do what his will was telling it to do. “The mind commands the body, and it obeys instantly; the mind commands itself, and is resisted.” The reason, he decided, was that he only half wanted it. A divided will is a weak will.

His old habits were still pulling at him, “muttering as it were behind my back.” He imagines them whispering: “Dost thou cast us off? and from that moment shall we no more be with thee for ever?” And underneath them a deeper voice: “Thinkest thou, thou canst live without them?”

On the other side he pictured a dignified, joyful figure he called Continency, surrounded by young men and women, widows and older people who had found self-control, not by their own strength but by God's. She seemed to say, “cast thyself fearlessly upon Him, He will receive, and will heal thee.”

The storm broke. Augustine moved away from Alypius so he could cry alone, threw himself down under a fig tree and wept. “How long, how long, 'to-morrow, and tomorrow?' Why not now? why not is there this hour an end to my uncleanness?”

Then he heard it. From a house nearby, a child's voice, boy or girl, he couldn't tell, chanting over and over: “Take up and read; Take up and read.” He tried to think whether children sang that in some game, and couldn't remember any. He remembered how Antony had been converted by hearing a Gospel verse read aloud as if it were spoken to him. So he stopped crying, went back to where Alypius was sitting with the book of Paul's letters, opened it, and read the first words he saw:

“Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, in concupiscence.”
“No further would I read; nor needed I: for instantly at the end of this sentence, by a light as it were of serenity infused into my heart, all the darkness of doubt vanished away.”

He marked the page and calmly told Alypius. Alypius asked to see it and read the next line, “him that is weak in the faith, receive.” He took that for himself, and joined Augustine without any fuss. It was the summer of 386, and Augustine was thirty-one.

Then they went inside and told Monica. Augustine writes that “she leaps for joy, and triumpheth, and blesseth Thee.” God had given her more than she had asked for. Her son was now standing “in that rule of faith,” exactly where her dream had shown him, years before.

Don't take the wrong lesson from this. The point isn't to wait for a mysterious voice or to open the Bible at random for instructions. That verse landed because Augustine had been reading, listening, arguing and being prayed for for years. The garden was the end of a long road. But the moment of surrender was real, and it came when he stopped saying “tomorrow” and said “why not now?”

One thing to do this week: read Romans 13:8–14, the passage around Augustine's verse, slowly, twice. Then pick one practical way to “make not provision for the flesh”: remove one thing that makes your “not yet” easy.

study_questions.answer: He read the next words, “him that is weak in the faith, receive,” applied them to himself, and calmly joined Augustine in his decision.

fields.title: At the Window in Ostia
fields.body_html:
“But as it is written, Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him.” — 1 Corinthians 2:9 (KJV)

Augustine didn't storm out of his job. He waited a few weeks until the grape-harvest holidays and then quietly resigned. Chest pains had made teaching hard anyway, which gave him an honest excuse. He, Monica, Alypius, his son and some friends went to stay at a borrowed country house. There he read the Psalms and wept over them.

The next spring, back in Milan, he was baptised by Ambrose, together with Alypius and his son Adeodatus, who was nearly fifteen. Augustine was amazed by the boy's mind. “Excellently hadst Thou made him,” he writes, and he says the ideas given to Adeodatus in a dialogue they wrote together were really the boy's own. But he also tells us, simply, “Soon didst Thou take his life from the earth.” Adeodatus died young, a few years later. At the services in Milan Augustine wept again: “How did I weep, in Thy Hymns and Canticles”.

They set off home for Africa and stopped at Ostia, the port of Rome, to wait for a ship. Here Augustine pauses to tell us about his mother. As a girl she had slowly slipped into a secret drinking habit, a sip at a time, until a servant girl in a quarrel called her a “wine-bibber” and she stopped for good. She married a hot-tempered husband who was unfaithful to her, yet she won him to faith before he died. She was a peacemaker who never repeated angry words from one person to another.

One day at Ostia, mother and son stood alone at a window looking out over a garden, talking about what heaven will be like. As they talked, their minds rose past everything in the world, past sun and stars, past their own thoughts, toward God himself, until for a moment “we slightly touched on her with the whole effort of our heart,” the eternal Wisdom of God. Then they came back down to ordinary words. Monica said:

“Son, for mine own part I have no further delight in any thing in this life. What I do here any longer, and to what I am here, I know not, now that my hopes in this world are accomplished. One thing there was for which I desired to linger for a while in this life, that I might see thee a Catholic Christian before I died. My God hath done this for me more abundantly, that I should now see thee withal, despising earthly happiness, become His servant: what do I here?”

About five days later she fell ill with a fever. She had always wanted to be buried beside her husband in Africa, but now she turned to her sons. “Lay,” she said, “this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.” When friends asked if she was afraid of dying so far from home, she said, “Nothing is far to God.” On the ninth day she died. She was fifty-five, in her fifty-sixth year; Augustine was thirty-two.

When she died, Adeodatus cried out loud. The adults hushed him, and Augustine forced back his own tears through the funeral, thinking a believer shouldn't weep. Inside he was breaking. He went to the baths, hoping it would ease the sadness, and was “the same as before I bathed.” He slept, and when he woke he finally let himself cry, “for her and for myself.” He asks his readers: if anyone thinks it was a sin that “I wept my mother for a small portion of an hour”, the mother “who had for many years wept for me that I might live in Thine eyes”, let him not mock, but pray.

Faith doesn't switch off grief. Augustine thought it should, and he was wrong, and he admits it. You can believe someone is with God and still sob that they aren't with you.

One thing to do this week: tell someone who loves you what they mean to you, this week, in words, not just a heart emoji. Don't wait for a window in Ostia.

study_questions.question: What happened at the window in Ostia?
study_questions.answer: Augustine and Monica talked about eternal life, and their minds rose beyond all created things until they briefly touched God's eternal Wisdom. Afterwards Monica said she had nothing left to live for in this world.

study_questions.question: What was Monica's last request?
study_questions.answer: Not to worry about where her body was buried, but to remember her at the Lord's altar wherever they were. “Nothing is far to God,” she said.

study_questions.question: Why did Augustine hold back his tears, and what did he decide later?
study_questions.answer: He thought weeping didn't fit a believer whose mother had died well. Later he let himself weep and wrote that no one should mock him for crying over the mother who had wept for him for years.

fields.title: Memory, Time and Rest
fields.body_html:
“There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.” — Hebrews 4:9 (KJV)

The story ends at Ostia. But the Confessions has four more books, and they surprise most readers. Augustine stops telling what he was and starts telling “what I now am.” He is a bishop, and he admits he is still tempted: to eat for pleasure rather than need, to be nosy (even a lizard catching flies can steal his attention from prayer), and most of all to love praise. He's honest about that: “I am delighted with praise, but with truth itself, more than with praise.”

Then he explores memory. He calls it “the fields and spacious palaces of my memory,” full of every place, face, smell and fact he has ever known. He is amazed that he can't get to the bottom of his own mind. “And men go abroad to admire the heights of mountains, the mighty billows of the sea ... and pass themselves by.” Searching through it all, he realises God isn't just one memory among others. God is above his mind, and had been calling to him all along. That leads to the book's most famous prayer:

“Too late loved I Thee, O Thou Beauty of ancient days, yet ever new! too late I loved Thee! And behold, Thou wert within, and I abroad, and there I searched for Thee; deformed I, plunging amid those fair forms which Thou hadst made. Thou wert with me, but I was not with Thee.”
“Thou calledst, and shoutedst, and burstest my deafness. Thou flashedst, shonest, and scatteredst my blindness. Thou breathedst odours, and I drew in breath and panted for Thee. I tasted, and hunger and thirst. Thou touchedst me, and I burned for Thy peace.”

Book XI asks a question that sounds easy: what is time? “If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.” The past is gone and the future isn't here, so where are they? His answer is that they live in the mind: “a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future.” In other words, memory, attention and expectation. Someone once asked what God was doing before he made the world. An old joke answered, “He was preparing hell (saith he) for pryers into mysteries.” Augustine won't mock a serious question. He answers that time itself is something God made, so there was no “before” for God to fill. God lives in an eternal now. We live stretched out and scattered: “my life is but a distraction.” Christ gathers us back together.

Books XII and XIII read the first chapter of Genesis slowly. Augustine doesn't claim to have every answer, and he warns against people who love their own reading of Scripture “not because it is truth, but because it is theirs.” Then he finds in creation a picture of the whole book. Everything moves toward its proper place, as a stone falls and a flame rises. “My weight, is my love; thereby am I borne, whithersoever I am borne.” What you love is what pulls you, where you end up. And he ends by looking forward to “the peace of the Sabbath, which hath no evening,” when we “shall rest in Thee also in the Sabbath of eternal life.”

So the book closes where it opened. The restless heart of the first page finally has a resting place. The last words are a promise from Jesus, turned into a prayer for anyone still looking: “so shall it be received, so shall it be found, so shall it be opened.”

That's the Confessions for you, in one line. Your heart will love something, and what it loves will carry it somewhere. You can spend years, as Augustine did, searching “abroad” for what was “within” all along. Or you can start knocking now.

One thing to do this week: find ten quiet minutes, with no phone, and ask yourself Augustine's question: what do I love most, and where is it carrying me? Then turn his last line into your own prayer: “Let me ask, seek and knock, and find you.”

study_questions.question: What does Augustine mean by “Thou wert within, and I abroad”?
study_questions.answer: That God was close to him the whole time, but he kept searching for happiness outside himself in created things, so he missed him.

study_questions.question: How does Augustine describe past, present and future?
study_questions.answer: As three kinds of present in the mind: a present of things past (memory), of things present (attention, or “sight”), and of things future (expectation).

study_questions.question: What does “My weight, is my love” mean?
study_questions.answer: Just as a stone falls and fire rises to their places, what you love pulls you and carries you where you go. Love decides your direction.
